California Baptist enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 25-8 overall and 15-5 against WAC competition, then added the WAC tournament title with an 86-72 win over Utah Tech on March 13 and a 63-61 championship win over Utah Valley on March 14. The NCAA bracket placed CBU as a No. 13 seed against No. 4 Kansas on March 20 in San Diego. The baseline profile is clear: this is a veteran, guard-led team with one elite shot-maker, a strong rebounding identity, and a defense that wins by shrinking the arc and finishing possessions on the glass rather than gambling for steals. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/calbaptist.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Offensively, CBU is built around Dominique Daniels Jr. controlling the ball late, then surrounding him with secondary spacers and interior rebounders. Daniels averages 23.2 points, 3.7 rebounds and 3.2 assists, and he used 577 field-goal attempts and 216 free-throw attempts through 33 games, by far the largest offensive burden on the roster. Martel Williams is the secondary perimeter scorer at 12.7 points and 4.9 rebounds, while Jayden Jackson gives them a third guard who will fire from deep; Jackson has attempted 152 threes in 27 games, nearly 5.6 per game, and made 54. Team-wide, CBU averages 73.0 points, shoots 43.2 percent from the field, 33.7 percent from three, and gets to 15.4 made free throws per game. The structure is not beautiful-motion offense: only 10.3 assists per game and a 0.8 assist-turnover ratio say this is a play-finishing team driven by individual creation, paint pressure, and second shots. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/calbaptist.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Specific tendencies show up in the game data. Against Utah Tech on January 21, CBU scored 44 points in the paint and 18 second-chance points in a 73-64 win, despite making only 5-of-17 from three. That is a strong indicator of their preferred interior route: Daniels drives, the bigs crash, and wings like Williams clean up. In that same game, CBU won the glass 40-36 and got 13 offensive rebounds, another marker of their half-court identity. When they need spread floor offense, Jackson and Jordan Muller are the release valves; Jackson is at 35.5 percent from three overall and Muller has made 32 threes. In late-clock situations, the ball predictably returns to Daniels. The best named example is January 24 versus Utah Valley, when Daniels scored a school-record 47 points in a 78-71 overtime win, including the driving layup with less than five seconds left in regulation to force overtime pressure onto UVU. On January 31 at UT Arlington, Daniels scored 13 overtime points in an 87-77 win, with Jayden Jackson adding 19 and Williams 11, showing the three-guard finishing group CBU trusts most. ([wacsports.com](https://wacsports.com/boxscore.aspx?id=7ltyipP022aUJKmSgYVs3wXi7up73ghniwD5ElWyd07J7BNseBaMQePf0fY%2F3yUPoLKU89tKqTsIOzgHNTx49iWu6ARk9zoePbd7Bx3uie4sN01ymkepU%2FOPPiB1U3KArYfDGqsOAhbRjTD9%2BSxMzmVkeEePl2bpUc14DplbqAJhkFKVOVBvs%2FAqy9hX0bzA&path=mbball))

Defensively, Rick Croy’s team plays a conservative, physical style. The clearest statistical markers are opponent shooting numbers: CBU holds opponents to 41.7 percent from the field and 29.7 percent from three overall; in conference-only games those improve to 40.4 percent overall and 27.9 percent from three. They do not generate many steals, only 5.5 per game, so this is not a high-pressure turnover scheme. Instead, they defend actions to tough twos, rebound the miss, and keep the three-point line clean. Their 7.4 rebound margin and 39.9 rebounds per game are central to the defense. Against Utah Valley in the WAC title game, that defensive patience held UVU to 61 points, and in the regular-season home win over Abilene Christian on February 7, CBU survived 65-63 by again finishing possessions late. The March 5 rematch with ACU was the extreme version: CBU won 87-48, proof that when their physicality sets the tone early, they can bury a league opponent. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/calbaptist.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Croy’s coaching philosophy is visible in both lineup use and adjustment history. He has leaned heavily on experienced guards and accepted low-assist offense in exchange for dependable decision-making from Daniels. Documented adjustments show up in results after early conference trouble: CBU opened WAC play 1-3 with losses at Utah Valley on December 29, at UT Arlington on January 1, and at Tarleton on January 3, then responded by winning 14 of its next 17 games entering Selection Sunday. The Utah Valley split is especially revealing. CBU lost 73-66 in Orem on December 29, then beat UVU 78-71 in overtime on January 24, then lost 65-46 in Orem on February 19, then beat UVU 63-61 for the WAC title on March 14. That sequence suggests real game-to-game tactical adaptation by Croy and staff rather than a one-off upset. The March 14 title game also included a documented in-game emotional adjustment: down seven with just over two minutes left, Croy said “the talk in the huddles was incredible,” and Daniels scored CBU’s final nine points, all on threes, to complete the comeback. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/calbaptist.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Clutch execution is one of CBU’s best tournament-selling points. On January 24, they beat Utah Valley 78-71 in overtime behind Daniels’ 47 points and his late regulation layup. On January 31, they won 87-77 in overtime at UT Arlington, with Daniels scoring 13 points in OT alone. On February 5, they escaped Tarleton 56-55. On February 7, they held off Abilene Christian 65-63. On March 14, they trailed Utah Valley by seven in the final three minutes and still won 63-61, with Daniels scoring the final nine points and the go-ahead three with just over 10 seconds left. Those are not vague “battle-tested” references; they are repeated, score-specific close-game wins in January, February, and March. ([cbulancers.com](https://cbulancers.com/news/2026/1/24/mens-basketball-daniels-jrs-historic-night-lifts-the-lancers-to-victory?utm_source=openai))

Key players start with Daniels, the WAC Player of the Year. The conference announced on March 10 that he averaged 22.6 points per game in the regular season, 23.8 in WAC play, and produced 21 games of 20-plus points. Through the WAC tournament he was up to 23.2 points per game overall. His standout moments are obvious: 47 against Utah Valley on January 24, 28 at UT Arlington on January 31, 26 against Utah Tech on January 21, and 23 in the WAC final on March 14. Martel Williams is the second scorer and a key two-way wing; he averages 12.7 points and 4.9 rebounds, and his size helps CBU rebound from the guard line. Jayden Jackson averages 9.3 points and is their most volume-oriented spacer after Daniels, with 54 made threes; he scored 19 at UT Arlington on January 31. In the frontcourt, Thomas Ndong averages 5.0 points and 6.6 rebounds, Bradey Henige 4.9 and 5.5, and Jonathan Griman 6.1 and 5.9; those three embody the committee-rebounding approach that lets CBU play small-guard offense without being physically overwhelmed. ([wacsports.com](https://wacsports.com/news/2026/3/10/basketball-m-cbus-dominique-daniels-jr-voted-2025-26-wac-mens-basketball-player-of-the-year.aspx))

Notable wins: 69-61 at UC Irvine on November 7 showed they could win away from Riverside against a quality West Coast opponent. A 75-69 road win at Oregon State on November 29 was another strong nonconference data point. The January 24 Utah Valley win revealed Daniels’ takeover ceiling and CBU’s ability to win an overtime game against the eventual regular-season champion. The March 14 win over Utah Valley revealed their highest-end trait: late-game shot-making under pressure. Notable losses matter too. The 91-60 loss to BYU on December 3 showed what happens when CBU’s guards face a high-major athlete/size gap and the offense cannot create enough easy twos. The 78-70 loss at Colorado on December 1 was more respectable and suggested they can hang physically for stretches. The February 19 loss at Utah Valley, 65-46, revealed the downside of their offense: if Daniels is contained and the half-court game bogs down, they do not have enough natural playmaking to manufacture points from flow. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/calbaptist.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

As for Rick Croy’s NCAA tournament history, at the Division I level this 2026 bid is his first NCAA tournament appearance with California Baptist. CBU’s official bio documents that he led the program to NCAA Division II tournament appearances every season from 2014 through 2018, highlighted by a 2017-18 West Regional championship and a trip to the Division II Elite Eight. That matters in a scouting sense: while this is his first Division I NCAA tournament game, it is not his first postseason run with win-or-go-home pressure. ([cbulancers.com](https://cbulancers.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/coaches/rick-croy/611))

Bottom line: Cal Baptist is a dangerous 13-seed because it has the exact traditional upset ingredients older analysts trust: a lead guard who can own the final four minutes, a coach with a clear identity, a team that rebounds at a plus-7.4 margin, and a defense that holds opponents under 30 percent from three. The weaknesses are equally concrete: low playmaking volume, turnover vulnerability at times, and offensive drought risk if Daniels is forced into hard twos without foul-line relief. If this becomes a tight game in the last five minutes, CBU has more evidence than most mid-majors that it can execute under pressure. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/calbaptist.sidearmsports.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

California Baptist enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament profile range as a strong mid-major winner with a noticeably split résumé: better on results than on pure predictive efficiency. As of games through March 15, 2026, Warren Nolan’s comparison page lists the Lancers at 25-8 overall with a NET rank of 98, KPI 83, SOR 85, WAB 76, BPI 137, KenPom 106, and Bart Torvik 96. Their average result-based ranking is materially better than their average predictive ranking, which is the first important takeaway: the résumé says fringe top-100 tournament-quality team, while possession-based systems see something more like a low-100s club. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))

Strength of schedule is a major part of that gap. On the Warren Nolan team sheet, California Baptist’s NET strength of schedule is 215 and its non-conference NET SOS is 274; the corresponding RPI SOS marks are 254 overall and 350 in non-conference play. That is a soft schedule by at-large standards, and it helps explain why a 25-8 record did not push the Lancers much higher in NET. The team sheet also shows almost no top-end résumé juice: 0-1 in Quadrant 1, 2-4 in Quadrant 2, 5-3 in Quadrant 3, and 18-0 in Quadrant 4. In other words, they handled weak opponents reliably but did not accumulate many high-value wins. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=California-Baptist))

The broad statistical picture available publicly suggests a defense-first, grind-it-out team that wins by controlling lower-tier opponents rather than overwhelming them. ESPN’s team page lists California Baptist at 72.8 points per game and 68.8 points allowed per game, with only 10.4 assists per game. That assist figure is extremely low nationally and hints at an offense that is relatively individual-shot driven, not especially fluid, and probably prone to possessions that end late in the clock. Their scoring rank on ESPN is only 304th nationally despite the 25-win record, reinforcing the idea that this is not a high-octane attack. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2856/california-baptist-lancers?utm_source=openai))

The best available possession-based evidence from public sources points to an offense that is competent but not elite and a defense that is more bankable. Bart Torvik’s ranking on the Warren Nolan comparison page puts CBU 96th, while KenPom is slightly lower at 106 and BPI much lower at 137. That spread matters. When Torvik and KenPom both place a team around the top 100 while BPI sits outside the top 130, the most natural read is that California Baptist looks respectable in game control and efficiency margin against its league slate, but lacks the athlete/shot-quality indicators that more skeptical models reward. Put differently: the Lancers are good enough to beat teams they should beat, but the underlying numbers do not scream upset threat against top-40 opponents. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))

Exact season-long adjusted offensive efficiency, adjusted defensive efficiency, and tempo values were not fully accessible in the open web sources returned, but the directional evidence is still useful. Sports-Reference advanced game logs and individual box pages show CBU repeatedly playing games in the high-60s to low-70s possession environment and producing offensive ratings that swing sharply with shooting variance. In wins over Utah Valley and Utah Tech, for example, team offensive efficiency snapshots reached 104.3, 107.7, and similar territory, while poorer nights such as the Tarleton loss produced only 80.9 points per 100 possessions. That volatility is consistent with a team whose offense depends heavily on making enough jump shots rather than generating a steady diet of rim pressure and assisted layups. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/boxscores/2025-12-29-02-utah-valley.html?utm_source=openai))

On the Four Factors, the game-level samples suggest a mixed profile. In better performances, California Baptist has posted strong effective field goal rates — for instance a .571 eFG in a road win at Utah Valley and .509 in a win at Utah Tech. But in losses or offensively constrained games, the eFG can crater; the Tarleton home loss showed just a .455 eFG and a 17.2% turnover rate with a very low free-throw rate of .109. That last number is especially telling. The available box-level evidence suggests CBU is not a heavy foul-drawing team, and that aligns with the eye-test implication from their low assist volume and modest scoring. When they are not making threes, they can bog down badly. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/boxscores/2025-12-29-02-utah-valley.html?utm_source=openai))

The available game logs also imply moderate-to-high three-point dependence. In several representative games, CBU’s three-point attempt rate sat around .250 to .328, then spiked as high as roughly .435 in the overtime loss at Tarleton when the Lancers attempted 39 threes on 51 field-goal attempts. That range suggests a team comfortable leaning into perimeter volume, especially when game state demands catch-up offense. Because their free-throw generation does not appear consistently strong from the box-level samples, three-point shotmaking becomes disproportionately important to their offensive ceiling. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/boxscores/2025-12-29-02-utah-valley.html?utm_source=openai))

Rebounding looks more solid than flashy. ESPN has California Baptist tied 31st nationally in rebounds per game at 40.6, and game-level advanced pages show some strong defensive rebounding performances, such as a 75.9% defensive rebound rate against Utah Valley and 81.8% against Utah Valley in the December meeting. That suggests the defensive glass is one real strength, which fits the broader profile of a team that protects itself against second-chance damage and keeps scores manageable. Offensive rebounding appears more variable: in some strong games the Lancers were above 20% OR%, but in others they were nearly absent on the offensive glass. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2856/california-baptist-lancers?utm_source=openai))

Recent form is encouraging. ESPN’s March 5 preview listed California Baptist at 21-8, 11-5 in the WAC at that time, and said the Lancers were 8-2 over their last 10 games, averaging 70.3 points, 36.0 rebounds, 8.6 assists, 4.3 steals, and 4.1 blocks while shooting 40.0% from the field. The shooting percentage there is not attractive, but the 8-2 run says the defense and rebounding floor held up even without beautiful offense. That is a classic warning sign for opponents who assume a top-100 mid-major must be offense-led. CBU’s recent success came despite ugly shotmaking efficiency, not because of it. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/preview/_/gameId/401805211?utm_source=openai))

So where do the numbers diverge from conventional wisdom? The conventional take on a 25-win WAC team is often that it must be an efficient, well-spaced upset candidate. The numbers say something subtler. California Baptist’s résumé metrics are decent, but the predictive metrics are lukewarm. Their schedule strength is weak. Their offense is less polished than the record implies. Their assist rate and scoring output suggest limited half-court creation. Yet the same data also says they are disciplined enough to avoid bad losses, rebound well enough to survive mediocre shooting nights, and defend well enough to keep games in range. That combination makes them more dangerous in ugly tournament games than in track meets.

Bottom line: California Baptist’s 2026 profile is that of a solid but imperfect top-100ish team nationally, with NET 98, KenPom 106, BPI 137, and Torvik 96. The Lancers appear more reliable on defense and on the glass than on offense, carry a soft schedule, and enter March with strong recent form but limited evidence of top-end shot creation. If they spring a tournament surprise, it will probably come via a slow-possession, low-efficiency game where their rebounding and defense flatten a more talented opponent’s margin for error. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))
matchup-analyst:
Cal Baptist enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a 25-8 team that won the WAC tournament and drew No. 4 seed Kansas in the first round on Friday, March 20, 2026. Their profile is clear: they are guard-driven, half-court oriented, rebound well for a mid-major, and lean heavily on one elite on-ball creator, Dominique Daniels Jr. Daniels played 36.2 minutes per game and produced 23.2 points, 3.2 assists, and 577 field-goal attempts, by far the largest usage footprint on the roster. No other Lancer averaged even 13 points. Martel Williams was second at 12.7 points, while the frontcourt scoring was much lower: Jonathan Griman 6.1, Devon Malcolm 5.9, Thomas Ndong 5.0, and Bradey Henige 4.9. That distribution strongly indicates a star-guard offense first and a complementary big rotation second. ([cbulancers.com](https://cbulancers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Style of play: Cal Baptist wants Daniels controlling possessions, getting downhill, living at the line, and creating enough paint pressure to open secondary threes or dump-offs. Daniels attempted 216 free throws and shot 81.5% there, while also taking 186 threes, so the offense is built around his ball dominance across all three scoring levels. Team-wide, CBU scored 73.1 points per game through nine games, then 73.2 points per game over 32 games, but the assist load stayed modest: 11.2 assists per game early and 11.3 for the full season. That low assist volume relative to scoring suggests a lot of self-created offense rather than a pass-heavy motion attack. Daniels alone took 32.2% of the team’s shots while on the floor sample shown in cumulative stats, and 67.8% of his own attempts were twos, reinforcing that the engine is a downhill isolation/ball-screen scorer, not a five-man equal-opportunity system. ([cbulancers.com](https://cbulancers.com/documents/download/2025/12/4/1206_Utah.pdf))

Which tactics disrupt that style? The evidence says physical point-of-attack defense, early help, and schemes that turn Daniels into a high-volume, low-efficiency scorer while shrinking driving lanes. In the Feb. 19 loss at Utah Valley, Daniels scored only 12 on 3-of-16 shooting and CBU shot 29% as a team with 20 turnovers in a 65-46 collapse. In the Jan. 1 loss at UT Arlington, Daniels still got 25, but the rest of the offense stalled; CBU had only one assist from Daniels, shot 23% from three, and lost 63-51 despite holding UTA to 35% shooting. That is the blueprint: load to Daniels, stay attached to spot-up help, and make secondary Lancers beat you. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/game/_/gameId/401805201/ca-baptist-utah-valley))

Press and zone vulnerability: the strongest available evidence points to ball-pressure vulnerability more than pure zone vulnerability. Cal Baptist’s full-season turnover count was 80 for Daniels alone and 48 for Jordan Muller, 38 for Jayden Jackson, 32 for Griman, 31 for Henige, and 30 for Ndong, while the team’s assist output remained limited. In losses where opponents sped up the possession math, the turnovers spiked: 23 at Utah Valley on Dec. 29, 17 at UT Arlington on Jan. 1, and 20 at Utah Valley on Feb. 19. Utah Valley is the clearest named example because it beat CBU twice in the regular season by forcing those 23 and 20 turnover games, then lost in the WAC title game once CBU cut that number to 13. Against Utah Valley in the March 14 WAC final, CBU still shot only 38% and Daniels needed 25 shots for 23 points, but the reduced turnover total let them survive 63-61. There is not enough primary-source evidence in the available 2025-26 game data to claim a specific zone weakness with confidence, but aggressive pressure clearly bothered them. ([cbulancers.com](https://cbulancers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Preferred pace and how to force the opposite: CBU is more comfortable in lower-possession, grind-out games. Their scoring average was only 73.2, their defense allowed 68.6, and they won multiple slow games such as 58-55 vs Southern Utah on Jan. 10, 56-55 vs Tarleton State on Feb. 5, and 63-61 vs Utah Valley in the WAC championship. When games became more open against high-major athleticism, they bled points: 91-60 at BYU on Dec. 3, 91-85 at Utah on Dec. 6, and 88-83 at Eastern Washington on Dec. 12. To force the opposite of CBU’s comfort zone, you want misses turned into early offense, made baskets inbounded quickly, and defensive rebounding that eliminates their half-court reset and second-shot rhythm. The best example is Utah’s 91-85 win: Utah shot 49%, got to 37 free throws, and led 96% of the game, preventing CBU from dictating a slow, controlled script. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/2856/california-baptist-lancers))

Size and athleticism mismatches by position: at point guard, Daniels is productive but undersized at 5-foot-10, so long guards can contest him late and switch onto him without giving up size elsewhere. At the two/wing spots, CBU starts 6-foot-4 Jayden Jackson and 6-foot-3 Martel Williams, but neither is an overpowering downhill wing scorer; Jackson shot 32.5% overall despite hitting 35.5% from three, which means length can bother him inside the arc. Jordan Muller is a 6-foot guard off the bench but shot just 30.5% overall. In the frontcourt, CBU has real size: Ndong is 6-foot-10, Griman 6-foot-11, Henige 7-foot-0, Garcia 7-foot-0, and D’Amelio 6-foot-9. The issue is not raw height but offensive polish and mobility. Ndong averaged only 5.0 points, Henige 4.9, and Garcia 2.4. Against athletic high-major fronts, the bigs are more useful as rebounders and finishers than as self-creators. Utah exposed that dynamic by winning despite being out-rebounded 47-30 because CBU’s size did not translate into enough efficient interior offense beyond Daniels’ drives. ([cbulancers.com](https://cbulancers.com/sports/mbball/roster))

Isolation vs. team offense tendencies: Daniels attempted 577 shots, or 32.2% of all CBU field-goal attempts credited in his usage share sample, and 10.6% of his shots were threes made, while the team’s assist rate stayed low at 11.3 assists per game. Daniels also had 103 assists against 80 turnovers, meaning the primary creation burden sat with him rather than being spread across multiple initiators. Williams had only 50 assists in 32 games; Jackson 48 in 27 games; Muller 62 in 33 games but on low efficiency. The offense is therefore much closer to creator-centric than team-flow-centric. A fair evidence-based estimate from usage and assist distribution is that Cal Baptist is substantially more isolation/advantage-creation dependent than a typical high-assist motion offense. ([cbulancers.com](https://cbulancers.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Transition offense and defense frequency: the available primary sources do not publish explicit possession-type frequency splits for CBU transition offense/defense, so I cannot truthfully assign exact transition percentages from the sources retrieved. What can be said from game evidence is that CBU performs better when games stay in the half court and worse when opponents force them into scramble possessions. The clearest proxy is turnover-driven pace distortion: 23 turnovers at Utah Valley, 20 at Utah Valley in the rematch loss, and 17 at UT Arlington all coincided with offensive outputs of 66, 46, and 51 points. By contrast, in the WAC semifinal against Utah Tech, when CBU kept turnovers to 12 and shot 50% overall and 53% from three, it scored 86. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/game/_/gameId/401805156/ca-baptist-utah-valley))

Coaching adaptability: Rick Croy’s staff does show game-to-game adjustment evidence, even if “mid-series” is not a college format. The best example is Utah Valley. CBU lost 73-66 on Dec. 29 with 23 turnovers, then lost 65-46 on Feb. 19 with 20 turnovers and Daniels at 3-of-16, but in the March 14 WAC title game they won 63-61 while cutting turnovers to 13 and winning the free-throw battle 10-of-11 to 14-of-24. That is not cosmetic; it reflects a meaningful tactical adjustment toward possession security and a lower-variance game. Another example is Utah Tech: CBU lost 70-65 on Feb. 14 while shooting 29%, then beat Utah Tech 86-72 on March 13 by shooting 50% overall and 53% from three, with Daniels exploding for 41. The staff clearly found better spacing and shot quality in the rematch. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/game/_/gameId/401805198/ca-baptist-utah-tech))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Cal Baptist, you must load up on Dominique Daniels Jr. with length at the point of attack, send early nail help on his drives, and rotate out to Jackson and Williams rather than over-helping to low-usage bigs. You must pressure their guards without gambling recklessly, because the named losses show CBU becomes vulnerable when turnovers reach the high teens or 20s. You must also play faster than they want: rebound and run after both makes and misses, because their best wins are grind games and several losses came when the game opened up. Offensively, attack Daniels’ size at 5-foot-10 with bigger guards, and force CBU’s big front line to defend in space rather than sit near the rim and rebound. Finally, do not let their size fool you into playing slow. Their bigs rebound, but the offense still runs through one small, high-usage guard. If you turn Cal Baptist into a second-side decision-making team instead of a Daniels shot-creation team, the efficiency drops sharply, as shown in the Utah Valley and UT Arlington losses. ([cbulancers.com](https://cbulancers.com/sports/mbball/roster))
